nodes.name: Carbon cloth pretreatment and TiO2 seed formation
nodes.procedure: Carbon cloth (WOS 1011) was further treated with nitric acid (HNO3). A piece of carbon cloth (1 by 1 cm²) was soaked in isopropanol containing 75 mM titanium butoxide for 3 min. The precursor was dried at 60°C and then annealed at 400°C with heating rate of 2°C/min for 2 hours in air to form a thin layer of TiO2 seeds.

nodes.name: Hydrothermal TiO2 nanorod growth and calcination
nodes.procedure: The carbon cloth with TiO2 seeds was transferred in Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave and immersed in a solution containing 5 ml of 6M HCl and 100 μl of titanium butoxide. Subsequently, the autoclave was heated at 150°C for 8 hours. After that, the hydrothermally treated carbon cloth was calcined at 400°C with a heating rate of 10°C/min for 2 hours in air.

nodes.name: TiO2-x formation by reduction
nodes.procedure: The TiO2 nanorod array was annealed at 700°C for 4 hours in H2/Ar flowing gas to prepare the defective TiO2 (named as TiO2-x) nanorod array.
nodes.source_text: Synthesis of TiO2-x nanorod array... annealed at 700°C for 4 hours in H2/Ar flowing gas...

nodes.name: IrTiO2-x impregnation-calcination
nodes.procedure: The piece of carbon cloth loaded with TiO2-x nanorod array was immersed in H2IrCl6 solution (0.5 mg/ml) for 4 hours. The IrTiO2-x was obtained by calcining the precursor sample at 300°C with heating rate of 5°C/min for 2 hours under argon atmosphere.

nodes.name: IrTiO_2

nodes.characterization_summary: EPR signal assigned to oxygen vacancy confirms presence in TiO_{2-x} nanorods.
nodes.evidence_snippet: the TiO_{2-x} nanorods with oxygen vacancy was successfully obtained via the calcination of TiO_2 nanorod array at 700°C for 4 hours in H_2/Ar flowing gas, which is confirmed by the electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signal assigned to oxygen vacancy (fig. S16)

properties.features: IrO2 shows baseline, IrO2-x shows peak at g≈2.00 and negative features

nodes.characterization_summary: TiO_{2-x} shows typical rutile structure (JCPD #21-1276) mixed with small amount of anatase phase (JCPD #21-1272); IrTiO_{2-x} XRD pattern is consistent with TiO_{2-x} support with no characteristic Ir diffraction peaks detected.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The x-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern of the TiO_{2-x} nanorods displays a typical rutile structure (JCPD #21-1276) mixed with a small amount of anatase phase (JCPD #21-1272) (fig. S17)... the XRD pattern of IrTiO_{2-x} is consistent with TiO_{2-x} support (fig. S17), and no characteristic diffraction peak related to Ir can be detected, implying the high dispersion of Ir in the catalyst

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM images show TiO_{2-x} nanorods have diameters ranging from 50 to 100 nm and length of around 2 μm; morphology unchanged after Ir introduction.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images show that TiO_{2-x} nanorods have diameters ranging from 50 to 100 nm and a length of around 2 μm (fig. S18). The morphology of TiO_{2-x} nanorods keeps unchanged after the introduction of Ir

nodes.characterization_summary: Ir content in IrTiO_{2-x} catalyst measured as 14.2 μg·cm^{-2}.
nodes.evidence_snippet: the element content of Ir in the catalyst was measured to be 14.2 μg·cm^{-2} by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES; table S5)

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM images show well-ordered lattice fringe (0.321 nm) corresponding to (110) plane of rutile TiO_2 with isolated bright dots (Ir atoms) randomly scattered on TiO_{2-x} support.
nodes.evidence_snippet: High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images of IrTiO_{2-x} present that the well-ordered lattice fringe (0.321 nm) corresponds to the (110) plane of rutile TiO_2, and isolated bright dots (Ir atoms) are randomly scattered

properties.description: Iridium oxide thin film or variant (ITO possibly, with variable oxidation state)

nodes.characterization_summary: EPR spectra of IrTiO_{2-x} confirm prominent existence of oxygen vacancies after Ir overgrowth.
nodes.evidence_snippet: EPR spectra of IrTiO_{2-x} further suggests the prominent existence of oxygen vacancy after overgrowth of Ir (Fig. 4B)

nodes.characterization_summary: Ir 4f XPS spectrum of IrTiO_{2-x} shows binding energy peaks at 62.25 eV (Ir 4f_{7/2}) and 65.14 eV (Ir 4f_{5/2}), indicating Ir^{4+} oxidation state.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure S20 shows the XPS spectra of Ir 4f for IrTiO_{2-x} and IrTiO_2 catalyst. The binding energy peaks at 62.25 and 65.14 eV belong to Ir 4f_{7/2} and Ir 4f_{5/2}, respectively, indicating that the oxidation state of Ir is 4+

nodes.characterization_summary: Ir L3-edge XANES white line intensity of IrTiO_{2-x} coincides with commercial IrO_2, demonstrating Ir mainly exists in 4+ valence state.
nodes.evidence_snippet: the white line intensity of IrTiO_{2-x} almost coincides with the commercial IrO_2, demonstrating that the valence state of Ir mainly exists in 4+

nodes.characterization_summary: EXAFS shows no Ir-Ir peak at 2.51 Å but dominant Ir-O peak at 1.63 Å, indicating atomic dispersion of Ir species.
nodes.evidence_snippet: For IrTiO_{2-x}, there is no obvious peak at 2.51 Å (for Ir-Ir scattering in metallic Ir), but the dominant peak around 1.63 Å ascribed to the Ir-O bond can be observed, indicating the atomic dispersion of the Ir species

nodes.characterization_summary: Double-layer capacitance (Cdl) from CV with variable scan rates estimates ECSA; IrTiO_{2-x} shows higher ECSA than IrTiO_2 (table S6).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Electrochemically active surface areas (ECSAs) were estimated by double-layer capacitance (Cdl) measurements from cyclic voltammetry with variable scan rates (fig. S23 and table S6), showing that IrTiO_{2-x} has a higher ECSA than IrTiO_2

nodes.characterization_summary: EIS shows lower charge transfer resistance (R_ct) for IrTiO_{2-x} indicating more efficient charge transfer.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The lower charge transfer resistance (R_ct) of IrTiO_{2-x} obtained from electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analysis... demonstrates more efficient charge transfer
